AgentSSL: Can MLE Agents Leverage Unlabeled Data?

Ethan Lin ††thanks: Equal contribution. Affiliation: Cornell University    Akanksha Sarkar11 1 Project website: https://codiscovery.ai/AgentSSL Affiliation: Cornell University    Ziang Liu Affiliation: Cornell University    Kristin Branson Affiliation: Howard Hughes Medical Institute    Jennifer J. Sun Affiliation: Cornell University
Abstract

Applying machine learning systems to new domains introduces bottlenecks in both labeled data acquisition and manual pipeline engineering. While recent MLE agents show promise in automating pipeline design, they have been studied almost exclusively in fully supervised settings, leaving them untested in realistic regimes where labeled data is scarce but unlabeled data is abundant. In this work, we introduce Agentic Semi-Supervised Learning (AgentSSL), framing SSL as a program search problem and studying how agents navigate this space under limited supervision. We find that even under weak feedback and matched compute, agents can synthesize code that combines and adapts established SSL techniques, exceeding the strongest human-engineered baselines in 8 of 12 settings by up to +21.8%. However, our results identify program selection as a critical bottleneck in AgentSSL, where performance drops by as much as 47% when selecting based on the agent’s feedback metric. To systematically study this bottleneck, we introduce ProgramSelectBench, a large-scale benchmark with a combined total of 16,977 agent-generated and human-engineered SSL programs, and evaluate both unsupervised and active program selection methods. We further evaluate AgentSSL on real-world ecology detection tasks, highlighting the opportunities and challenges of transferring agent-discovered strategies beyond controlled benchmarks.

1 Introduction

“What we observe is not nature itself, but nature exposed to our method of questioning.”
— Werner Heisenberg

Modern machine learning depends on two costly inputs: (1) labeled data to provide supervision, and (2) human engineering to design the inductive biases and pipelines (e.g. architectures, augmentations, and training strategies) required to extract signal from that data Hestness et al. (2017); Kaplan et al. (2020).

Recent agent-based approaches target engineering cost by reframing ML pipeline development as program search, iteratively generating and refining executable code based on task feedback. The capabilities of these agents have improved significantly. For example, on MLE-Bench Chan et al. (2024), a benchmark of 75 Kaggle competitions, the top agent performance has risen from a mean percentile rank of 45.2% Toledo et al. (2025) to 83.1% Hambardzumyan et al. (2026) in just a single year, driven by a rapidly expanding ecosystem of agents Jiang et al. (2025); Liu et al. (2025); Nam et al. (2025); Zhang et al. (2026); Hambardzumyan et al. (2026). Despite this success, there remains a fundamental limitation in our method of questioning: existing agentic benchmarks overwhelmingly assume fully supervised settings. MLE-Bench primarily contains tasks with thousands to millions of training samples. As a result, agents are optimized to search over programs under the assumption that labeled data is abundant.

This assumption rarely holds in practice. In many real-world domains (including scientific discovery, medical diagnostics, and environmental monitoring), labeled data is scarce and expensive while unlabeled data is abundant. This raises a fundamental question: can agent-based systems remain effective in data-scarce regimes by leveraging unlabeled data?

This places the problem naturally within semi-supervised learning (SSL), where a small labeled set is paired with a much larger unlabeled corpus. Despite strong results on classical benchmarks such as CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 Krizhevsky and Hinton (2009), SSL remains difficult to deploy in practice since these methods are highly sensitive to how well the data distribution matches the algorithm’s underlying assumptions (e.g. cluster structure, consistency under augmentation, etc.) Zhu (2005a); Yang et al. (2023). As a result, the methods often require significant dataset-specific tuning. This brittleness suggests that deploying SSL can be viewed as a search problem over a large design space spanning graph-based label propagation Zhu (2005a), pseudo-labeling Lee (2013), consistency regularization Tarvainen and Valpola (2017), and many more Zhu (2005a); Yang et al. (2023).

In this work, we introduce Agentic Semi-Supervised Learning (AgentSSL), formulating the domain-specific application of SSL as a program search problem. We decompose this problem into two core challenges: (1) program discovery, where agents must discover effective SSL programs under limited feedback, and (2) program selection, where a single program must be identified from the discovered candidates without a large labeled validation set.

To study program discovery, we investigate two unsupervised feedback approaches for guiding agentic search. We find that, even when unsupervised feedback is weakly or even negatively correlated with final accuracy, agents can still discover SSL programs that are competitive with, and in 8 of 12 settings outperform, recent SSL baselines. Through extensive empirical and qualitative analysis, we find that agents explore and combine diverse ideas spanning decades of SSL research, with the strongest agent-generated solutions effectively leveraging both unlabeled data and domain-specific structure.

Despite discovering strong SSL programs, agents face a significant challenge in reliably selecting the best programs. This reflects a longstanding challenge in practical SSL: selecting methods and hyperparameters without access to a reliable labeled validation set Oliver et al. (2019); Zhang et al. (2025). We evaluate two promising approaches. First, we find that unsupervised metrics enable effective selection when underlying assumptions hold. Second, when unsupervised metrics fail, actively allocating labels to program selection can outperform allocating them to training. To facilitate further research, we introduce ProgramSelectBench (Appendix C), a large-scale program selection benchmark comprising 16,977 precomputed programs representing over 10,000 GPU hours of compute.

Finally, we evaluate AgentSSL on animal detection tasks from real-world ecology pipelines, showing both its potential to reduce annotation cost and the instability of deploying agent-discovered SSL strategies outside controlled classification benchmarks. To summarize, our contributions are:

  • •

    We introduce Agentic Semi-Supervised Learning (AgentSSL), formulating SSL as agentic search over the space of SSL programs.

  • •

    We show that MLE agents can autonomously discover diverse, domain-adapted SSL programs that effectively leverage unlabeled data, achieving performance competitive with established SSL baselines, outperforming them in 8 of 12 settings.

  • •

    We identify reliable program selection as an open problem for AgentSSL, and release ProgramSelectBench, a large-scale program selection benchmark with 16,977 programs of human baseline and agent solutions.

  • •

    We evaluate AgentSSL on real-world ecology detection tasks, demonstrating the potential and challenges for agents to reduce annotation-cost in practice.

2 Related Work

2.1 Automating Machine Learning Engineering (MLE)

Automating MLE has long been a goal of the ML community. Traditional AutoML methods, including hyperparameter optimization Akiba et al. (2019), pipeline search Olson and Moore (2019), and neural architecture search (NAS) White et al. (2023); He et al. (2021), typically formulate automation as optimization over predefined search spaces, such as model architectures, training procedures, and hyperparameters. While effective in many settings, these methods often require substantial human specification of the search space and optimization objective.

Recent LLM-based MLE agents offer a more flexible alternative by searching over executable programs and iteratively proposing, executing, debugging, and refining code using feedback from the environment Novikov et al. (2025); Jiang et al. (2025); Liu et al. (2025); Nam et al. (2025); Zhang et al. (2026); Hambardzumyan et al. (2026). Because these agents combine many interacting design choices, controlled evaluation frameworks are important for isolating the effects of search policies, feedback signals, and other components Toledo et al. (2025); Yang et al. (2025). We use Aira-Dojo Toledo et al. (2025) as such a test harness, providing a consistent environment for studying these design choices in our SSL setting.

Existing MLE agents are also typically evaluated on supervised-learning benchmarks with substantial labeled training and validation data. MLE-Bench Chan et al. (2024) evaluates agents across 75 Kaggle competitions, while AIRS-Bench Lupidi et al. (2026) considers challenging tasks drawn from ML research papers. In contrast, we evaluate MLE agents in a data-efficient setting where labeled data is limited, making program discovery and program selection under weak feedback itself a central challenge.

2.2 Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL)

SSL studies how to leverage unlabeled data together with limited labeled data. We briefly review its major paradigms since our agent builds on both traditional and modern SSL methods.

Classical SSL methods. Classical methods impose assumptions on how labeled and unlabeled examples should relate Zhu (2005b). For example, graph-based methods encourage connected examples on a similarity graph to share labels Song et al. (2021); low-density separation methods, such as transductive SVMs, encourage decision boundaries to avoid dense regions Chapelle and Zien (2005).

Deep SSL methods. Deep SSL implements similar assumptions through neural training objectives Yang et al. (2023). Pseudo-labeling and self-training use model predictions on unlabeled data as targets. Consistency regularization enforces invariance to augmentations. Early methods like Π\Pi-Model Laine and Aila (2017) and Mean Teacher Tarvainen and Valpola (2018) used consistency between different trained networks as an objective. FixMatch Sohn et al. (2020) combines several SSL approaches, including weakly augmented pseudo-labeling, confidence thresholding, and strongly augmented consistency training. Subsequent methods such as SoftMatch Chen et al. (2023) refine this through adaptive thresholds, curriculum selection, or confidence weighting. FineSSL and V-PET are recent SSL methods tailored for foundation models, either through addressing biases in foundation-model adaptation Gan and Wei (2024) or ensembling complementary pseudolabels from multiple PEFT methods and foundation-model backbones Zhang et al. (2025).

2.3 Unsupervised and Active Model Selection

Model selection without a large labeled validation set remains an open challenge in data-efficient settings. Unsupervised model selection replaces labeled validation performance with statistics computed from model predictions or learned representations. Many such metrics were originally developed in other contexts, including classical clustering and statistics Fowlkes and Mallows (1983); Vinh et al. (2009); Halkidi et al. (2002); Caliński and Harabasz (1974), representation learning Garrido et al. (2023), and domain adaptation or data-efficient learning Cui et al. (2020); Saito et al. (2021). Recent work has repurposed and evaluated these signals as unsupervised validation criteria in unsupervised domain adaptation Ericsson et al. (2023) and SSL Zhang et al. (2025), but their reliability depends on assumptions that may not hold consistently across datasets or models Kay et al. (2025); Ericsson et al. (2023). An orthogonal direction is active model selection, which uses a limited annotation budget to identify the best model. Existing approaches include uncertainty- or variance-driven methods that prioritize labels most useful for reducing uncertainty in model performance estimates Kossen et al. (2021); Matsuura and Hara (2023), as well as probabilistic approaches that model uncertainty over candidate model quality and use this posterior to guide label acquisition Kay et al. (2025); Okanovic et al. (2024). Both directions provide promising avenues for improving model selection in AgentSSL when a large labeled validation set is unavailable.

Benchmarking model selection. Existing evaluations of model selection under limited supervision remains limited, both in size and diversity of candidate models. In particular, active model selection methods are typically evaluated over a finite set derived from following the same fine-tuning procedure on different pre-trained models and hyperparameters Okanovic et al. (2024); Kay et al. (2025). This leaves open how well existing selection methods scale to settings where candidate solutions may differ substantially in architectures, training procedures, and hyperparameters.

3 Problem Setup

3.1 SSL Problem Formulation

In the SSL setting, each task provides a labeled dataset L={(xiℓ,yiℓ)}i=1|L|L=\{(x_{i}^{\ell},y_{i}^{\ell})\}_{i=1}^{|L|} and an unlabeled dataset U={xiu}i=1|U|,U=\{x_{i}^{u}\}_{i=1}^{|U|}, where typically |L|≪|U||L|\ll|U| with the goal of constructing a prediction function h:𝒳→Yh:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow Y that achieves high performance on a held-out test distribution.

Rather than restricting the solution space to a particular parameterized model trained with a fixed SSL objective, we define a solution more generally as a program 𝒜:(L,U)↦h,\mathcal{A}:(L,U)\mapsto h, which takes the labeled and unlabeled data as input and returns a predictor. This formulation includes conventional deep SSL methods that learn parameters θ\theta of a model fθf_{\theta} using both LL and UU, while also allowing broader strategies such as classical transductive or graph-based SSL methods.

3.2 AgentSSL Problem Formulation

We formulate AgentSSL as an agentic search problem over the space of SSL programs, comprising two core challenges: (1) program discovery, where an agent iteratively generates and refines candidate programs under limited feedback, and (2) program selection, where a single program must be identified from the discovered candidates for deployment under label scarcity.

Program Discovery. We define the solution space as a set of programs 𝒮={𝒜:(L,U)↦h}\mathcal{S}=\{\mathcal{A}:(L,U)\mapsto h\}, where each program specifies a complete learning procedure for constructing a predictor from the available data. Following prior work Toledo et al. (2025), we model agentic search as growth of a directed acyclic graph over programs: greedy and MCTS expand single nodes and induce trees, while evolutionary crossover combines two parents into one child. At iteration tt, the agent maintains a directed graph Gt=(Vt,Et),G_{t}=(V_{t},E_{t}), where each node v∈Vt⊆𝒮v\in V_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{S} represents a candidate SSL program and each directed edge (vi,vj)∈Et(v_{i},v_{j})\in E_{t} represents a transformation from one program to another. At each iteration, the agent selects one or more existing programs, applies an operator to produce a new candidate program, evaluates it using a feedback signal, and adds the resulting node to the search graph. Concretely, an AgentSSL search procedure is specified by the tuple (F,πsel,𝒪,πop,M),\left(F,\pi_{\mathrm{sel}},\mathcal{O},\pi_{\mathrm{op}},M\right), where FF is a fitness function, πsel\pi_{\mathrm{sel}} is a node selection policy, 𝒪\mathcal{O} is a set of program transformation operators, πop\pi_{\mathrm{op}} is an operator selection policy, and MM is the LLM. We use a fixed operator set with Draft, Debug, Improve, and Analyze operators (Appendix H.1).

Program Selection. Following program discovery, we obtain a pool of candidate programs 𝒫⊆𝒮\mathcal{P}\subseteq\mathcal{S}. The goal of program selection is to identify the best-performing program 𝒜∗∈𝒫\mathcal{A}^{*}\in\mathcal{P}, defined as 𝒜∗=arg⁡max𝒜∈𝒫⁡𝒬⁡(𝒜),\mathcal{A}^{*}=\arg\max_{\mathcal{A}\in\mathcal{P}}\mathcal{Q}(\mathcal{A}), where 𝒬⁡(𝒜)\mathcal{Q}(\mathcal{A}) denotes the performance of the predictor produced by program 𝒜\mathcal{A} on the test distribution. However, true performance is unknown, and the limited labeled data available in SSL makes it difficult to reliably identify 𝒜∗\mathcal{A}^{*}. We therefore study program selection under different information constraints. Unsupervised selection chooses programs using label-free metrics Zhang et al. (2025) computed on an unlabelled validation set. Active model selection chooses programs by actively querying a limited number of test labels.

Evaluation. We evaluate these two challenges separately. To assess program discovery, we measure oracle performance, defined as the test performance of the best program in the discovered pool, 𝒬⁡(𝒜∗)\mathcal{Q}(\mathcal{A}^{*}). This measures the quality of the best discovered solution, independent of our ability to select it. To assess program selection, we measure selection regret, defined as Rsel=𝒬⁡(𝒜∗)−𝒬⁡(𝒜s),R_{\mathrm{sel}}=\mathcal{Q}(\mathcal{A}^{*})-\mathcal{Q}({\mathcal{A}}_{s}), where 𝒜s{\mathcal{A}}_{s} is the program chosen by a selection method. Lower regret indicates that the selection method more reliably identifies high performing programs from the discovered pool.

3.3 Agent Design Space

The AgentSSL formulation exposes several design choices that can affect how agents explore the space of SSL programs. We focus on three components that are especially relevant to our study: the fitness function, the search strategy, and the language model.

Fitness Functions (FF). The fitness function defines the feedback signal received by the agent during search. This is especially important in SSL, where labeled validation data is scarce. We consider two families of feedback signals: (i) noisy validation, where a small labeled subset is held out for evaluation, and (ii) unsupervised metrics, Zhu (2005a); Chapelle et al. (2009); Zhang et al. (2025) where programs are scored using label-free statistics computed from predictions or representations on unlabeled data. Noisy validation provides direct supervised feedback but can have high variance in low-label regimes. Unsupervised metrics instead test whether agents can search effectively using only structure in unlabeled data. The construction of the noisy validation signal introduces a tradeoff between robustness and evaluation cost: stronger estimates such as cross-validation reduce variance but substantially increase program evaluation time. In our experiments, we tune this configuration separately for each dataset, though we view automated adaptation of this tradeoff as an interesting direction for future work. More details about the metric calculation in Appendix A.2.

Search Strategies (πsel\pi_{\mathrm{sel}}). The search policy πsel\pi_{\mathrm{sel}} determines which nodes v∈Vtv\in V_{t} in the search graph Gt=(Vt,Et)G_{t}=(V_{t},E_{t}) are expanded at each iteration. Different strategies induce different exploration–exploitation tradeoffs: greedy selects the highest-score programs under FF, evolutionary search mutates a population of candidate programs, and MCTS balances exploration and exploitation through tree search. We study how πsel\pi_{\mathrm{sel}} affects performance and diversity of discovered SSL strategies.

Language Model Backbone (MM). The language model MM instantiates the program transformation operators 𝒪\mathcal{O} by generating modifications to existing programs. Given a node v∈Vtv\in V_{t} and operator o∈𝒪o\in\mathcal{O}, the model proposes a transformed program v′v^{\prime}. Differences in coding ability and prior SSL knowledge can therefore affect both the quality and diversity of discovered solutions.

AgentSL To establish a simple agentic baseline, we perform experiments using agentic supervised learning (AgentSL) by removing the unlabeled data as input to the agent.

4 Experiment Design

Datasets. We conduct our experiments using the image classification SSL setting from recent work on semi-supervised learning with foundation models Zhang et al. (2025). Following the VTAB protocol Zhai et al. (2019), it includes six datasets across three categories: Natural (DTD Cimpoi et al. (2014), SUN397  Xiao et al. (2010)), Specialized (RESISC45 Cheng et al. (2017), Retinopathy (RETINO) Dugas et al. (2015)), and Structured (CLEVR-Count (CLEVR) Johnson et al. (2017), KITTI  Geiger et al. (2013)), spanning texture recognition, scene understanding, remote sensing, medical imaging, synthetic reasoning, and autonomous driving. For each dataset, we evaluate two class-balanced settings, corresponding to different numbers of labeled examples per class. For robustness, since few-shot results can be sensitive to which examples are labeled, we generate three random splits for each dataset and shot setting and evaluate all agent and baseline methods on each split.

Baselines. We compare agents against six baselines: Supervised, FixMatch, SoftMatch, FineSSL, PET, and V-PET. Supervised baseline measures performance without unlabeled data; FixMatch and SoftMatch represent standard deep SSL methods; FineSSL, PET, and V-PET represents SSL strategies tailored for foundation models. For all baselines, we follow the original protocol from prior work Zhang et al. (2025), focusing on the subset of their experiments that use CLIP ViT-B-16 Radford et al. (2021) and DINOv2-B Oquab et al. (2024) and fine-tune with LoRA Hu et al. (2021). See Appendix B for more details.

Agent Implementation. We build on AIRA-Dojo Toledo et al. (2025) as an agentic program-search framework and introduce a new SSL task interface within it. Agents receive a task description together with the labeled set LL and unlabeled set UU, and propose executable programs that map these data inputs to a predictor hh (Figure 2). Candidate programs are executed in an isolated Apptainer environment using a user-defined fitness evaluation program, and the resulting execution logs, errors, and fitness scores are returned to the agent as feedback for subsequent search steps.

Agent Details. To make agent-discovered programs directly comparable to the baselines, we constrain the agent search space in our image classification experiments. Agents thus only use CLIP ViT-B-16 and DINOv2-B backbones and are provided access to the same parameter-efficient fine-tuning library used in the baseline evaluations. We initialize each search with a simple supervised warm-start program to focus the agent on exploring SSL strategies rather than rediscovering the experimental infrastructure. We evaluate agents using two different feedback metrics, Unsupervised (U) and Noisy-validation (N), and use a greedy search policy. See Appendix A for more details.

Search Budget. We allocate agent search budgets based on the computational cost of the corresponding baseline SSL methods for each dataset. Since candidate evaluation time varies substantially with dataset size, this scaling gives agents more wall-clock time on larger datasets. For the smaller datasets, DTD, RESISC45, and KITTI, we run each agent for 8 hours on an NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada Generation GPU. For the remaining larger datasets, we run each agent for 15 hours on either an NVIDIA H100 GPU or an NVIDIA RTX 6000 Blackwell Max-Q GPU. For a comparison between baseline and agent compute costs, see Appendix B.2.

Evaluation Protocol. For each dataset and shot setting, we construct three random splits, corresponding to different labeled and unlabeled sets (L,U)(L,U). We evaluate every baseline method and hyperparameter configuration on all three splits, and run one independent agent trajectory on each split. We define the "best" program as the program with the best average performance across all data splits. Thus, every agent-generated program is executed and evaluated on the other two splits as well.

5 Results

Across datasets and shot settings, AgentSSL discovers programs that are competitive with strong SSL baselines when programs are selected using oracle test performance (Table 1). This result shows that the agent search process is capable of discovering high-performing SSL programs even when feedback is weakly or even negatively correlated with test accuracy (Figure 7).

The gap between oracle and practical selection, however, highlights a central challenge for AgentSSL and SSL more broadly: identifying the best discovered program when validation feedback is weak. Table 2 reports practical selection regret when using the feedback metric for selection. When the metric is well correlated with test performance, much of the oracle performance is retained; when this alignment is weak, selection performance can degrade substantially. These results suggest that practical program selection is a major bottleneck for AgentSSL. We provide a comprehensive evaluation of all unsupervised selection metrics on ProgramSelectBench in Appendix C.

A limitation of unsupervised selection is that its metrics necessarily encode assumptions about what constitutes a good model. For example, several metrics assess properties of learned representations. However, the agent may discover programs that reuse the same frozen representation while applying different downstream SSL procedures. In such cases, representation-based metrics cannot distinguish between programs despite potentially large differences in predictive performance.

When unsupervised metrics fail, active model selection offers a promising alternative by using labels for selection. Under a fixed budget, we compare training on all labels with unsupervised selection against splitting labels evenly between training and active selection (Table 3). This allocation yields large gains where unsupervised metrics fail, though it costs accuracy where they already work. Active selection strategies carry their own tradeoffs. IID, ActiveTesting, and VMA perform well on average but have much higher variance across runs than probabilistic methods such as CODA (deterministic) and ModelSelector (Table 9). Conversely, CODA and ModelSelector can converge with fewer labels but can be unstable as labels accumulate (Figure 10). We provide further evaluation and analysis of active model selection on ProgramSelectBench in Appendix C.

6 Analysis

6.1 Can Agents Leverage Unlabeled Data?

We first study whether the discovered SSL programs actually make use of unlabeled data. To do this, we fix the top-performing program discovered by AgentSSL and vary only the size of the unlabeled corpus at evaluation time. Figure 3 shows that performance generally improves as more unlabeled data becomes available while keeping the labeled set fixed. This suggests that the discovered programs rely on structure present in the unlabeled data itself.

6.2 How Do Agents Use Unlabeled Data?

To qualitatively analyze the agent’s search space at scale, we use an LLM-as-judge pipeline to categorize the SSL strategies implemented across generated programs Zhou et al. (2025); Tong and Zhang (2024). Our goal is to characterize which methods agents discover and how broadly they explore the SSL design space. We define high-level SSL categories using six classical groups from Zhu (2005b) and four modern deep SSL groups from Yang et al. (2023). Category definitions, prompts, and implementation details are provided in Appendix D; all LLM-as-judge-derived claims are manually verified.

The left panel of Figure 4 shows that agents explore a broad range of SSL paradigms and often combine multiple strategies within the same program. Although the frequency of individual strategies varies across datasets and search strategies, diverse and hybrid exploration is consistent across settings; full distributions are provided in Appendix D.3. We further find that these programs can be complementary. Inspired by Zhang et al. (2025), the right panel of Figure 4 shows that high-performing programs based on different SSL strategies assign high-confidence pseudolabels to different subsets of unlabeled images. This suggests that future AgentSSL systems could use discovered programs not only as search candidates, but also as complementary pseudolabel generators.

6.3 Do Agents Adapt SSL to Different Domains Effectively?

One benefit of AgentSSL is the ability to discover dataset-specific learning strategies rather than relying on a single fixed SSL recipe. Figure 5 shows that programs discovered for one dataset often transfer poorly to others i.e., the strongest programs are adapted to their source domain.

A particularly illustrative example appears on Retinopathy (Appendix J.1). The best program does not train a classifier; instead, it combines frozen DINOv2 features, nearest-neighbor evidence, class prototypes, and an explicit ordinal bias. These choices align naturally with diabetic retinopathy, where labels represent ordered disease severity levels and images from similar severity stages may cluster in feature space. Despite avoiding parametric training, this program improves over the next-best baseline by 19%, illustrating how AgentSSL can discover domain-specific inductive biases rather than simply optimizing a generic SSL recipe.

7 Ablation

We analyze how different agent design choices affect behavior in AgentSSL. Specifically, we study two axes: (1) the underlying language model and (2) the search strategy. We evaluate each configuration using both final test accuracy and a diversity metric based on Jaccard dissimilarity Xuefei et al. (2025) using the LLM-as-judge derived method groups. A higher diversity score indicates that the agent explores a broader range of SSL strategies and implementation choices. Across experiments, we observe: different agent configurations often achieve comparable accuracy, but differ substantially in the diversity of SSL strategies they explore. This suggests that agent design choices primarily influence how the search space is traversed rather than simply determining the best final program.

LLM Backbone. We compare GPT-5.4 and Gemini-3.1 as the underlying program-generation models (Table 4). Both models achieve comparable accuracy across datasets, with GPT-5.4 slightly outperforming Gemini-3.1. However, Gemini-3.1 consistently produces higher diversity scores. This mirrors the trend: stronger exploration does not always translate into higher accuracy under constrained search budgets, but substantially changes the distribution of discovered SSL solutions.

Search Strategy. We compare greedy, MCTS, and evolutionary search across DTD, KITTI, and RESISC45 (Table 5). While all three strategies achieve similar accuracy ranges, they differ substantially in diversity. Evolutionary consistently produces the highest diversity scores, suggesting that population-based search encourages broader exploration. In contrast, greedy converges to narrower regions of the search space despite competitive accuracy, while MCTS lies between. These results suggest that under fixed compute budgets, the primary effect of the search strategy is not necessarily improving peak performance, but altering the breadth of SSL strategies explored during search.

8 Applying AgentSSL to Ecology Detection Tasks

We evaluate AgentSSL on detection tasks derived from two ecological pipelines, WildFin Grassick et al. (2026) and BuckTales Naik et al. (2024), where expert-trained detectors support downstream behavioral analysis and tracking for fish and antelope. We compare the ecologist baselines trained on the entire training split to solutions that only have access to 10% of the data for WildFin and 20% of the data for BuckTales. Additional dataset and experimental details in Appendix F.

The purpose of this case study is two-fold. First, we demonstrate a real-world setting where AgentSSL could significantly reduce both engineering and annotation cost. Second, we study whether the flexibility of MLE Agents enables the design of domain-specific SSL algorithms on tasks beyond classification that are significantly less studied. In a setting where it is unclear if unlabeled data is even useful, we additionally evaluate AgentSL, a subset of AgentSSL without access to unlabeled data, keeping the small labeled set. This comparison helps reveal whether a practical agent should exploit simpler supervised solutions or explore more uncertain strategies that leverage unlabeled data.

Figure 6 shows encouraging but task-dependent results. On WildFin, with just 10% of the total data, AgentSL and AgentSSL outperform the low-label expert baseline and approach the full-data expert pipeline. On BuckTales, both agents match the low-label expert baseline. We observe that even without a large validation set, agents can discover programs that match or exceed domain-expert solutions, and on WildFin demonstrates that agentic search can substantially reduce annotation cost.

The similar performance of AgentSL and AgentSSL across both domains also suggests that unlabeled data is not always the most valuable source of improvement. In practical settings where the utility of SSL is uncertain, strong supervised design choices may be as important as more exploratory strategies that leverage unlabeled data. Since AgentSL represents a restricted subset of the broader AgentSSL solution space, future systems should ideally search over both: exploiting simple supervised improvements when they are effective while exploring more uncertain, domain-specific uses of unlabeled data when they offer additional gains. More broadly, reducing annotation and engineering costs in scientific workflows will require agents to jointly optimize supervised design choices, SSL strategies, and domain-specific constraints.

9 Discussion and Conclusion

We introduced AgentSSL, which formulates semi-supervised learning as agentic program search. Under label scarcity, MLE agents generate SSL programs that beat tuned human baselines in 8 of 12 settings when the best program is known, but neither agents nor human pipelines can reliably pick that program without labels. We also introduced ProgramSelectBench (Appendix C), which makes this selection problem measurable, and our results show that when unsupervised metrics fail, labels spent on selection buy more accuracy than the same labels spent on training.

Limitations and future work.

First, SSL is not always preferable to supervised learning, especially when simple modeling or engineering choices provide comparable gains Oliver et al. (2019); on both ecology tasks, AgentSL matches AgentSSL. Because our instantiation biases search toward SSL strategies, future systems should treat whether to use unlabeled data as part of the search, balancing reliable supervised improvements against more uncertain uses of unlabeled data. Second, we use AIRA-Dojo as a controlled and standardized search framework, but MLE agents are rapidly improving. Stronger LLMs and harnesses may search more efficiently and discover better solutions, so we view our results as an initial agentic baseline rather than the performance ceiling of AgentSSL. Third, our search relies on weak feedback and measuring how search efficiency and final accuracy change as feedback gets stronger remains open. Finally, our comparison with human baselines (Table 1) highlights the challenges of selecting programs without labels. Stronger agents will not close this gap and may widen it: the more programs an agent generates, the larger the gap can grow between the best program and the one chosen without labels. Closing it calls for unsupervised and active selection methods that stay reliable across program families, for which ProgramSelectBench provides a testbed. More broadly, our results suggest that as agents make candidate programs cheap to generate, the bottleneck in AgentSSL shifts from building programs to choosing among them.

Appendix A Agent Details

A.1 Agent Hyperparameters

The MLE Agent search hyperparameters for each strategy are provided below:

  • •

    Greedy: 5 initial drafts, 5 improvement steps, debug probability of 1.0, and maximum debug depth of 5.

  • •

    MCTS: 5 children per expansion, UCT exploration constant of 0.25, and maximum debug depth of 20.

  • •

    Evolutionary: 5 individuals per generation, 100 generations, crossover probability of 0.5, and maximum debug depth of 10.

  • •

    LLM sampling: Draft, improve, and debug operators use temperature 0.6 and top-p=0.95p=0.95; analysis uses temperature 0.5.

A.2 Feedback Metric Details

Noisy Validation

One SSL feedback metric we test is a noisy validation metric. This is created by splitting the existing limited training set into train and validation. In order to manage variance due to limited size of the validation set, we perform kk-fold noisy validation to get better signal. However, because there is a tradeoff between reducing variance in performance estimates and managing compute time, we manually tune the kk hyperparameter per dataset. The exact fold number picked for each dataset in this work is listed below:

  • •

    DTD : 3-shot and 6-shot both have 3-fold noisy validation

  • •

    RESISC45 : 1-shot is not applicable for noisy validation and 2-shot has 2-fold validation

  • •

    SUN397 : 3-shot and 6-shot both have 3-fold noisy validation

  • •

    Retinopathy : 40-shot and 80-shot both have 1-fold noisy validation

  • •

    CLEVR : 10-shot has 5-fold and 20-shot has 4-fold noisy validation

  • •

    KITTI : 5-shot and 10-shot both have 3-fold noisy validation

Automatically determining the best kk value for a task or even dynamically determining the resources used to reduce uncertainty in performance estimates during search is an interesting future research direction.

Unsupervised Metrics

Inspired by prior work [59], we use an ensemble of different unsupervised metrics as feedback for the agentic search. Since different unsupervised metrics capture different properties of the learned representations and predictions, an ensemble should be able to balance these biases.

Because the metrics operate on different numerical scales, we map each score to [0,1][0,1] using predefined global bounds derived from its valid range, clipping values to those bounds before normalization. We deliberately restrict the ensemble to metrics with well-defined normalization ranges. The final unsupervised fitness score is the mean of the selected normalized metrics, yielding a single scalar objective for ranking candidate programs during search.

The ensembled unsupervised fitness score includes the following metrics:

  • •

    AMI [52]: mutual information between cluster assignments, corrected for chance.

  • •

    ARI [18]: pairwise agreement between cluster assignments, corrected for chance.

  • •

    V-measure [43]: entropy-based measure balancing cluster homogeneity and completeness.

  • •

    FMI [13]: agreement between clusterings based on pairwise precision and recall.

  • •

    Silhouette Score [44]: cluster compactness relative to separation from neighboring clusters.

  • •

    RankMe [15]: effective rank of learned representations as a proxy for representation quality.

  • •

    BNM [10]: nuclear norm of batch predictions, capturing discriminability and prediction diversity.

  • •

    SND [45]: local feature-space density measured through pairwise feature similarities.

These metrics have also been studied for unsupervised model selection in prior work  [12, 59]. However, they are not always correlated to test accuracy. In Figure 7, we see that both feedback metrics, unsupervised and noisy validation, can even be negatively correlated with test accuracy on datasets like KITTI and Retinopathy. We generally see a similar trend across all the unsupervised metrics as well as for other ensemble strategies like rank, which selects the program with the best average ranking across each metric [59].

A.3 Total Compute

We scale the agent search budget according to the computational cost of the corresponding SSL baselines, since candidate evaluation time increases substantially with dataset size. For the smaller datasets (DTD, RESISC45, and KITTI), each agent run is allocated 8 GPU hours on an NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada Generation GPU. For the larger datasets, each run is allocated 15 GPU hours on either an NVIDIA H100 GPU or an NVIDIA RTX 6000 Blackwell Max-Q GPU.

Across 6 datasets, 2 shot settings, and 3 random seeds, each agent setting comprises 36 runs: 18 with an 8-hour budget and 18 with a 15-hour budget. We evaluate two agent settings, unsupervised and noisy validation, for a total compute budget of 2×(18×8+18×15)=8282\times(18\times 8+18\times 15)=828 GPU hours. This number represents the amount of compute time taken to perform agent trajectories on a single seed. In our evaluation, we also compute every program on 2 additional seeds which triples the total compute cost to 2,484 GPU hours.

Appendix B Baseline Details

B.1 Methods and Hyperparameters

We evaluate the same supervised and SSL baselines described in the main text. For all baselines, we follow the training protocol and hyperparameter search space from prior work [59], using the authors’ released implementation. We consider configurations based on CLIP ViT-B/16 [42] and DINOv2-B [41], with parameter-efficient fine-tuning using LoRA [22], and reproduce the prescribed hyperparameter tuning procedure.

To reduce sensitivity to the particular labeled examples selected in the few-shot regime, we rerun every baseline across three independently sampled labeled/unlabeled splits for each dataset and shot setting. The original study reports results on a single labeled split. For each seed, agents and baselines are evaluated on the same labeled and unlabeled split, so comparisons are paired under identical data conditions. We report results aggregated across the three seeds.

This evaluation protocol requires a large number of trained models for each dataset and shot setting:

Accounting for all datasets, shot settings, random splits, and required pretrained/adapted models, we train 2,520 models for baseline results and 4,248 models in total when including the additional AdaptFormer supervised runs required to compute PET and V-PET.

B.2 Total Compute

The breadth of baseline algorithms and hyperparameter configurations makes the baseline evaluation substantially more computationally expensive than any individual AgentSSL search. As seen in Table 7, the total compute used to train and tune the baseline models far exceeds the total compute allocated to the agent experiments. Note that PET and V-PET include several other computationally expensive steps that we do not include.

Appendix C ProgramSelectBench: Details and Results

We compile and release ProgramSelectBench, a precomputed benchmark for unsupervised and active program selection consisting of 16,977 evaluated program instances across six classification datasets. ProgramSelectBench is constructed from the programs evaluated in AgentSSL, including both agent-generated programs and human-designed baselines. The benchmark provides a controlled setting for studying program selection independently of program discovery, allowing future work to evaluate selection strategies without the computational cost of generating and executing new programs. The benchmark is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/ethan-y-lin/ProgramSelectBench.

C.1 Selection task definition

A selection task consists of a pool of candidate programs ℋ={h1,…,hK}\mathcal{H}=\{h_{1},\ldots,h_{K}\}, evaluated on a common set of examples. The objective is to identify the program with the highest ground-truth accuracy without directly observing the full set of ground-truth labels. In unsupervised selection, methods may use the programs’ predictions and extracted features to estimate their relative performance. In active selection, methods additionally have access to a limited annotation budget and may actively query labels to distinguish between candidate programs. Selection performance is measured by the ground-truth accuracy of the selected program, or equivalently its regret relative to the best program in the pool.

C.2 Benchmark Details.

We organize ProgramSelectBench into 35 selection tasks corresponding to the dataset, shot, and evaluation settings considered in AgentSSL. Each task contains all evaluated program instances for the corresponding setting, including both agent-generated programs and human-designed baselines. Table 8 summarizes the number of programs in each task.

We treat programs trained on different labeled-data splits as distinct candidate instances. Although these instances may share the same algorithm and implementation, differences in training data can produce substantial variation in their predictions and test performance. Because each baseline configuration and agent-generated program is evaluated using three training splits, we include each trained instance as a separate candidate in the corresponding selection pool.

Figure 8 illustrates the distributions of program accuracy across the benchmark tasks. The tasks vary in both the number of candidate programs and the distribution of their performance, providing a range of selection problems. Furthermore, the benchmark is not restricted to the task partitions used in AgentSSL: any subset of programs evaluated on the same examples can define a new selection task, enabling the construction of alternative candidate pools. For example, we could construct a larger selection task on DTD by combining every shot and setting pools into a single large pool.

Released artifacts. ProgramSelectBench provides precomputed predictions and unsupervised evaluation metrics for all candidate programs. For each selection task, we aggregate the predictions of all programs on the corresponding test set into a single tensor file, allowing selection methods to efficiently load and compare the full candidate pool without executing individual programs. We additionally provide precomputed unsupervised metrics for each program to facilitate the evaluation of unsupervised selection methods. ProgramSelectBench also includes all agent-generated programs alongside textual descriptions of the corresponding method and implementation. We provide code for evaluating these programs and extracting their predictions and intermediate features. Similarly, we provide the code to evaluate all baseline methods as well and extract predictions and features. Although we have computed the features which are useful for unsupervised metrics, we do not include them in the benchmark release due to their substantially larger storage requirements.

C.3 Selection Results

For unsupervised selection, we evaluate all the unsupervised metrics discussed in Section A.2 on ProgramSelectBench. For active selection, we evaluate several active selection methods including ActiveTesting [28], VMA [34], CODA [27], ModelSelector [38], and an IID baseline. We evaluate each one for ten random seeds (except for CODA which is deterministic), taking the average performance across seeds, and use default hyperparameters. The number of iterations, or label budget, provided for each active selection algorithm and task is defined by:

min​(25,# of classes×# of training images per class)\text{min}(25,\text{\# of classes}\times\text{\# of training images per class})

The main selection results are shown in Figure 9. Similar to the results in Table 2, individual unsupervised metrics generally perform very poorly on all Retinopathy and KITTI tasks with some exceptions. We also see that even when dataset and shot are fixed, there is still high variance in the performance of unsupervised metrics across different program pools. For example, AMI, ARI, and FMI perform well on CLEVR (0 and 3% regret) for agent noisy validation tasks, however, on agent unsupervised tasks, they perform very poorly (15% and 39%). This inconsistency across datasets and even program pools suggests that using these metrics in practice may be unreliable.

Active Model Selection methods, with just 25 labels or less, have much smaller simple regret than the unsupervised selection methods. Notably, the IID baseline performs very well and even has the best average simple regret on the baseline tasks. Suprisingly, we also observe that the IID baseline actually also has smaller variance than ActiveTesting and VMA (Table 9).

We analyze the active model selection results more closely in Figure 10, where we plot the regret versus iterations where the iterations per task is defined by

min​(100,# of classes×# of training images per class).\text{min}(100,\text{\# of classes}\times\text{\# of training images per class}).

We can see that there is high variance across seeds on IID, ActiveTesting, and VMA, which lowers their real-world utility. CODA (which is deterministic) and ModelSelector exhibit much smaller variance, and often converge more quickly to zero regret, however are more unstable. For example, on the RETINO (40-shot) noisy validation task, both CODA and ModelSelector get to zero regret with less than 25 labels, but after 40 labels, they suddenly select a program with 30% worse accuracy.

Our benchmark results suggest that there is significant room for improving both unsupervised selection methods and active selection methods, which will greatly increase the practical performance of any data-efficient method.

Appendix D LLM-as-Judge Details and Results

We use an LLM-as-judge pipeline to analyze the programs produced during agent search at scale with GPT-5.4. Given a program as input, the judge extracts: (i) the models used, (ii) the high-level SSL method groups represented by the program, (iii) implementation-level details, (iv) whether the program performs training, and (v) a short rationale summarizing the previous choices. This structured representation lets us quantify which parts of the SSL design space agents explore, while preserving enough detail for manual validation. We show the high level method distribution results in this paper and will release all analysis output data and agent-generated programs.

D.1 High-Level SSL Method Groups

We categorize each program using a set of classical and modern SSL method groups. The classical groups are adapted from prior SSL surveys, which organize methods by assumptions about the data distribution, decision boundary, and relationship between labeled and unlabeled examples [63]. The modern deep SSL groups follow recent taxonomies that distinguish deep generative methods, consistency regularization, graph-based methods, pseudo-labeling, and hybrid approaches [56]. We additionally include contrastive learning because many modern programs use representation learning objectives over labeled and unlabeled data before or during downstream training [23] and we see this reflected in the agent outputs.

  • •

    Generative Models. Generative SSL methods model the joint distribution of inputs and labels, or the class-conditional data distribution, and use unlabeled data to improve estimates of the underlying data-generating process.

  • •

    Graph-Based Methods. Graph-based SSL methods construct a graph over labeled and unlabeled examples and propagate label information through the graph under the assumption that nearby or strongly connected examples should share labels.

  • •

    Avoiding Changes in Dense Regions. Low-density separation methods encourage decision boundaries to lie in low-density regions of the input or feature space, rather than cutting through clusters of unlabeled examples.

  • •

    Distribution Alignment. Distribution alignment methods adjust predictions, pseudo-labels, or learned representations so that the model’s predicted label distribution better matches a target prior or expected class distribution.

  • •

    Self-Training. Self-training methods iteratively train a model on labeled data, assign labels to unlabeled examples using the model’s own predictions, and retrain or refine the model using these pseudo-labeled examples.

  • •

    Co-Training and Multiview Learning. Co-training and multiview methods train multiple models or views of the data that exchange predictions, relying on complementary information across views to label unlabeled examples.

  • •

    Deep Generative Models. Deep generative SSL methods use neural generative models, such as VAEs or GANs, to learn latent structure from unlabeled data and improve supervised prediction.

  • •

    Consistency Regularization. Consistency regularization methods encourage a model to produce stable predictions under input perturbations, data augmentation, dropout, or other stochastic transformations.

  • •

    Deep Graph-Based Methods. Deep graph-based SSL methods combine neural representations with graph propagation, graph neural networks, or feature-space neighborhood structure to transfer label information across labeled and unlabeled examples.

  • •

    Pseudo-Labeling. Pseudo-labeling methods assign hard or soft labels to unlabeled examples using model predictions and then train on these pseudo-labeled examples, often with confidence thresholds or filtering.

  • •

    Contrastive Learning. Contrastive learning methods learn representations by pulling together positive pairs and pushing apart negative pairs, often using unlabeled data to improve feature quality before or during SSL.

Appendix E Diversity Metric Details

We measure the diversity of agent-generated programs following prior work [55], adapting their API-based Jaccard diversity metric to the high-level SSL method groups used in our analysis.

For each program ii, let SiS_{i} denote the set of high-level SSL method groups identified in that program by our LLM-as-judge pipeline. For two programs SaS_{a} and SbS_{b}, we compute their Jaccard dissimilarity as

Jδ​(Sa,Sb)=1−|Sa∩Sb||Sa∪Sb|.J_{\delta}(S_{a},S_{b})=1-\frac{|S_{a}\cap S_{b}|}{|S_{a}\cup S_{b}|}.

Given nn generated programs, the final diversity score is the mean pairwise Jaccard dissimilarity across all unique program pairs:

Diversity=1(n2)​∑a<bJδ​(Sa,Sb).\mathrm{Diversity}=\frac{1}{\binom{n}{2}}\sum_{a<b}J_{\delta}(S_{a},S_{b}).

Higher values indicate that the agent explores programs composed of more distinct combinations of SSL strategies, while lower values indicate that the generated programs rely on more similar sets of SSL methods.

Appendix F Ecology Experiment Details

F.1 Datasets

We select two ecological detection datasets to evaluate AgentSSL in real-world settings beyond classification.

WildFin [17]

WildFin is an in-the-wild fish video behavior classification dataset that is derived from a real-world ecology pipeline. The detection artifact from there dataset was obtained by ecologists hand-labeling bounding boxes for three species of interest (requiring over 320 hours of expert effort, yielding 21,116 expert-labeled boxes). An ecologist implemented a program using YOLOv8, trained on this data, and used that detector for downstream tasks like cropping specific fish for behavior studies. We received their exact program and obtained our baseline results by executing them on our random subsets of their data.

BuckTales [35]

BuckTales is a UAV-based wildlife dataset focused on blackbuck monitoring and downstream multi-object tracking. The detection dataset contains approximately 24,000 bounding boxes across six object categories. While the full dataset includes additional classes such as dogs and birds for behavioral analysis, the original study focuses just on the blackbucks in the context of MOT and Re-ID. We obtained the program for their evaluation directly from the authors and re-ran their experiments on our subsets on all classes.

F.2 Experiment Details

For each dataset, we used three random seeds to randomly sample subsets of the full training sets (10% of all images for WildFin and 20% of all images for BuckTales).

We execute the ecologist baseline program on all three of these random splits to produce the low-label domain expert baseline. We also execute the ecologist baseline programs on the entire training set to serve as the scientific success threshold, the threshold performance required to be actually used in the real-world scientific analysis pipeline.

We execute both AgentSL and AgentSSL using a greedy search policy and noisy validation feedback where 20% of the data provided to the agent is set aside for validation. We run each of these agents once on each of the three random splits.

Appendix G Agent SL vs. Agent SSL

Although SSL research generally focuses on methods that effectively leverage unlabeled data, choosing not to use the unlabeled data and instead performing supervised learning (SL) is also a valid strategy. From this perspective, SL can be viewed as a subset of the broader SSL solution space. Indeed, prior work has shown that, in many settings, well-tuned SL can perform comparably to state-of-the-art SSL methods [39]. To investigate this relationship in the context of AgentSSL, we conduct an ablation in which agents are not given access to unlabeled data. As shown in Table 10, under oracle selection, AgentSL performs comparably to AgentSSL, suggesting that the strongest supervised programs discovered by the agents can be as effective as those that explicitly leverage unlabeled data.

While AgentSSL is motivated in part by understanding how agents can leverage unlabeled data, our broader goal is to reduce the domain-specific engineering and annotation costs required to develop effective learning systems. If the best data-efficient solution for a particular task is simply a well-designed supervised learning pipeline, then this is a solution the agent should be able to discover. More broadly, we view the defining challenge of AgentSSL, and of the practical application of SSL more generally, as searching for effective programs in a regime with little or no validation data. Whether and how to leverage unlabeled data is therefore itself part of the search problem.
